evidence: The full mr̥ttikā entry gives Assamese, Bengali and Oriya māṭi “earth, soil, clay”, alongside Prakrit mattiyā/maṭṭiā. These eastern soil responses match the complete regional māṭi family, with survey dental t versus retroflex ṭ notation preserved. This family link leaves interlanguage transmission open; Turner’s separate uncertainty over Shina māṭi is not generalized to these eastern forms.

Full mudrā lists Prakrit muddiā, Punjabi mundī “ring”, Gujarati mū̃drī, Marathi mudī and Oriya mudi. The selected western/eastern survey mundī/muḍī/mundrī forms preserve that ring family, including source aspiration and optional nasal or r. The ancient head is itself probably an Iranian loan according to Turner; the modern link identifies its later Indo-Aryan continuations and does not erase that qualification. Extra diminutive material and potentially maṇḍala-derived forms are excluded.

Turner explicitly includes Oriya pilā “small; child” under *pilla, with Prakrit pella/pīlua and Bengali pil/children expressions. These adjacent eastern boy forms fit that full child word. The entry derives the older family from Dravidian; this reflex link concerns its later Indo-Aryan continuation, with Oriya-mediated regional transmission left open.

The full *dāṁṣṭra article includes its dāṭhikā/dāḍhiā beard branch and explicitly Bengali/Oriya dāṛ(h)i “beard, chin”. Hajong dadi matches this eastern chin/beard family with the survey d for the medial rhotic/retroflex segment. The link preserves Turner’s qualified expressive/contact discussion and the addendum’s alternative reconstruction; it is not an assertion that the head’s remote history is settled.

The full *dvālayati “kindles” entry gives Lahnda bālaṇ and Punjabi bālaṇā, and the addendum explicitly marks Sindhi bārṇū transitive “to burn”. Pothwari bāl is a transitive imperative with wood as its object, selecting this long-vowel causative family rather than intransitive *dvalati (6654).

Turner’s *trāgga/*tārga/*tāgra article explicitly has Punjabi tāgā/taggā “thread”, also Hindi, Bengali and Nepali tāgā, continuing Prakrit tagga. Pothwari tāɣā preserves the whole word with intervocalic g lenited to ɣ. The reconstruction alternatives remain alternatives within the chosen dictionary family; aspirated thāgā forms are excluded pending comparison with *dhāgga.
